strengths: R2E offers a coherent contribution to retrieval-based NLP: candidate-specific evidence retrieval, a set-transformer reasoner, and passage-level Shapley attribution produce inspectable entity rankings. Training with NULL evidence embeddings thoughtfully supports the interventions used for attribution.

The gene-ranking experiments provide substantive evidence of benefit. On Gene Description Facts, uncorrected R2E achieves 0.202 MRR versus 0.176 for MCS and 0.167 for MLM. Updating the retrieval corpus improves 2022 literature MRR from 0.205 to 0.219 without retraining, directly supporting the adaptability claim.

Document-level corpus splitting, training the retriever from scratch, temporal literature restrictions, and architecture ablations demonstrate methodological care. Reporting comparable performance on non-stratified literature also usefully identifies where the improvements occur.

The three evaluation datasets and detailed appendices covering architecture, hyperparameters, attribution algorithms, and annotation prompts are valuable. Templated genetics demonstrates flexibility, while the auditing experiment provides a concrete use for evidence attribution, with a modest reported AUROC improvement from 0.633 to 0.638.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is a decisive concern preventing a clear Findings recommendation. The Impact Statement explicitly withholds training data, code, and model weights, while Appendices B–C depend on licensed full texts and a proprietary entity linker. The methodological detail and public evaluation datasets help, but there is no reproducible public-data configuration demonstrating that the reported gains can be recovered without the unavailable pipeline.

The strongest performance claims need better-controlled comparisons. Appendix G derives frequency correction for the MLM, yet a corrected MLM baseline is not reported; this matters particularly for the gene-balanced evaluations. Clinical AUROC is nearly identical for R2E and MLM (0.632 versus 0.630), and non-stratified literature performance is comparable to MCS. A semantic-similarity baseline using the templated genetics would also help distinguish the benefit of semantic matching from the learned Reasoner.

The combined and audited clinical results are not established as temporally controlled forecasts. The pre-2005 restriction applies to literature, but the 2023 genetics resource and GPT-4 audit are not shown to respect the same information cutoff. This does not invalidate the literature-only experiment, but it limits the interpretation of the combined system as predicting outcomes from information available before the trials.

Clinical development status is an imperfect measure of therapeutic efficacy. Appendix O treats discontinued Phase II/III development as failure and pre-registration or later as success, while acknowledging commercial and molecule-specific causes of discontinuation. These results support retrospective discrimination among tested hypotheses more directly than claims about biological efficacy or discovery of novel targets.

Validation of explanation usefulness remains limited. Human checks cover only eight query–target pairs per task, with GPT-4 agreement of 71.5% and 82.2%, and no inter-annotator reliability assessment. Clinical Shapley–GPT-4 relevance AUROC is 0.665. The attributions are mathematically well-defined, but these relevance measurements do not establish their advantage over retrieval similarity or simpler attribution methods. Comparing audit selection strategies and expanding independent expert annotation would strengthen the central explanation claim.

Numerical and uncertainty reporting require clarification. Section 4.5.1 reports relative success of 1.92 with a 95% interval of (1.64, 1.77), which does not contain the estimate. Literature-only R2E-Corrected AUROC is 0.632 in Table 3 and 0.639 in Table S8 without an explicit explanation of the discrepancy. Most main comparisons lack confidence intervals or repeated-run variability, limiting assessment of the smaller gains.
